data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's 'Redundancy Paradox' argument substitutes an empirical claim for the comparative reasoning the problem requires. It asserts that beyond a certain scale the coordination layer becomes a single point of failure (SPOF), but it never establishes the covering principle: why the same complexity-driven coordination failure cannot arise inside a decentralized network that itself needs coordination/protocol layers (service discovery, routing, consensus on shared state). A decentralized mesh using a shared protocol for interoperability can contain the same coordination-class SPOF it attributes only to the monolith. By treating 'absence of a global coordination failure' as a property of decentralization rather than a contingent design feature, it begs the question against the monolith and ignores the problem's demand to identify what evidence would distinguish true independence from apparent uncorrelation. It gives no distinguishing evidence; it only posits a structural disadvantage.
